extracted.intended_audience: jurors (and trial judges) in federal patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions describing legal standards for proving infringement (including means‑plus‑function, direct and indirect), willfulness, and various invalidity defenses (written description, enablement, best mode, anticipation, statutory bars, obviousness). Intended to guide a jury's findings in a patent trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function claims (§112, ¶6)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish literal infringement of a means-plus-function patent claim, [the patent holder] must prove two things: (1) that the accused device employs a structure [act] identical or equivalent to the structure [act] described in the patent, and (2) that the relevant structure [act] in the accused device performs the identical function specified in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the structures are not identical, the patent holder must prove by a preponderance (more probable than not) that the accused structure is equivalent to the disclosed structure. Two structures are equivalent if a person of ordinary skill in the art would consider the differences insubstantial. Determine whether the accused structure performs the identical function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, or whether persons of ordinary skill would have considered the structures interchangeable at the time of patent grant. Note: §112, ¶6 requires identical, not equivalent function; equivalence under §112, ¶6 and the doctrine of equivalents are not coextensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — overview (inducing and contributory)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of indirect infringement: inducing infringement (encouraging or inducing others to infringe) and contributory infringement (contributing to others' infringement by supplying components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect infringement requires proof of a corresponding direct infringement for each instance. Inducing cannot occur unintentionally (it requires purposeful causing, urging, or encouraging). Contributory infringement requires additional component-specific elements (see separate criterion). Statutory sources: 35 U.S.C. §§271(b) and (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing patent infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A party induces patent infringement if it purposefully causes, urges, or encourages another to infringe. To prove inducement, the patent holder must prove it is more probable than not that: (1) the alleged infringer actively encouraged or instructed another person on how to [use a product or perform a process] in a way the jury finds infringes the patent claims; (2) the alleged infringer knew of the patent; (3) the alleged infringer knew or should have known that the encouragement or instructions would induce infringement; and (4) the other person infringed the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent holder must prove specific intent to induce infringement — knowingly inducing infringement, not merely knowingly inducing acts that constitute infringement. There must be proof of a direct infringement for each instance of indirect infringement. (See 35 U.S.C. §271(b).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — component requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement can occur when a party with knowledge of the patent supplies a part or component to another for use in a patented product, machine, or process. It arises only if the recipient infringes the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The supplied component must have three characteristics: (1) the component must be a material part of the invention; (2) the component must be especially made or adapted for use in a way that infringes the patent, and the supplier must know it was especially made for that use; and (3) the component must not have a substantial non-infringing use. A staple or commodity article with a number of non-infringing uses is not contributory infringement even if later used infringingly. (See 35 U.S.C. §271(c).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement (recklessness and state of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful infringement relates to whether increased damages should be awarded. To prove willful infringement, the patent holder must persuade the jury that it is highly probable that, before the complaint filing date, the alleged infringer acted with reckless disregard of the patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-part test for reckless disregard examines (a) the alleged infringer's conduct — whether it proceeded with allegedly infringing conduct with knowledge of the patent and in the face of an unjustifiably high risk of infringement of a valid patent — and (b) the alleged infringer's state of mind — whether the risk was known or so obvious that the alleged infringer should have known. Consider all facts including, but not limited to: whether the alleged infringer acted consistent with industry standards, and whether it intentionally copied without a reasonable basis a product/method covered by the patent as distinguished from trying to design around the patent. Willfulness ordinarily depends on prelitigation conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — general standard and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent invalidity is a defense to infringement. Even though the PTO allowed the claims, the jury and judge decide validity. The alleged infringer bears the burden of proving it is highly probable that the claims are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee note: although patents have a presumption of validity, instructing both the presumption and the 'highly probable' burden may confuse juries; this instruction omits explicit reference to the presumption. The alleged infringer must meet the heightened evidentiary burden ('highly probable') for invalidity defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement is satisfied if a person of ordinary skill reading the original patent application would recognize that the application described the invention as claimed, even if not using the exact words in the claim. It is adequate if it shows the inventor was in possession of the invention at the time the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that every aspect of the claim be explicitly discussed, as long as a person of ordinary skill would understand the aspect is implicit in the original application. The alleged infringer must prove it is highly probable the patent lacked an adequate written description. (Cited cases: Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle & Co., Enzo Biochem, Purdue, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (sufficiency to make and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the specification does not disclose sufficient information to enable one skilled in the field to make and use the claimed invention. The alleged infringer must prove it is highly probable that the claim was not enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are written for persons skilled in the art and need not state what such persons would likely know. The need for some experimentation does not necessarily mean lack of enablement. Factors to consider for undue experimentation include: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary; (2) amount of direction or guidance in the patent; (3) presence or absence of working examples; (4) nature of the invention; (5) state of the prior art; (6) relative skill of those in the art; (7) predictability of the art; and (8) breadth of the claims. (See In re Wands and cited authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor knew of a best way, or 'mode,' of making and using the claimed invention when filing the application, the specification must contain a description of that mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining best mode involves two questions: (1) At filing, did the inventor know of a mode of making or using the invention that the inventor considered better than any other (a subjective inquiry)? If no, stop — no best mode failure. (2) If yes, does the patent contain a description of that best mode sufficient to enable a skilled person to carry it out without undue experimentation (an objective enablement inquiry)? If both are proven highly probable, the claims are invalid. The purpose is to ensure full disclosure to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — novelty (public use/known or previously published)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated (not new) if all of its requirements existed in a single device or method that predates the claimed invention, or were described in a single prior publication or patent that predates the claimed invention. The alleged infringer must prove it is highly probable the claim was anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure in the prior reference need not use the same words as the claim, but all claim requirements must be present, either stated or necessarily implied, such that someone of ordinary skill could make and use the claimed invention. Ways to show anticipation include: prior public knowledge or use in the U.S., prior patent or printed publication anywhere in the world (if reasonably accessible), prior issued U.S. patent or published U.S. patent application (subject to applicable dates). If invention date is disputed, the jury must determine the date of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — made or invented by someone else (prior invention by another)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is anticipated if the invention was made or invented by someone else prior to the named inventor. The alleged infringer must prove it is highly probable the claim was anticipated by another's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways to show prior invention include: the claimed invention was already made by someone else in the U.S. before the relevant date (and not abandoned or secret); the named inventor learned of the invention from someone else; or inventorship disputes where the first to conceive and reduce to practice (with diligence where required) may be the first inventor. Use definitions: conception (mental part proven by complete disclosure), reduction to practice (tested to work or filing), and reasonable diligence (continuous work subject to ordinary interruptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars (timeliness / one-year bars)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be invalid if the applicant failed to meet statutory timing provisions — i.e., certain events occurred more than one year before the patent application filing date (statutory bars). For invalidity by a statutory bar, all claim requirements must have been present in a single prior art reference dated more than one year before the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways to show statutory bar (choose applicable): prior printed publication anywhere in the world more than one year before filing (reasonably accessible to interested persons); public or commercial use in the U.S. more than one year before filing (not primarily experimental use); sale or offer for sale in the U.S. more than one year before filing where the claimed invention was ready for patenting (actually built or sufficiently detailed drawings/descriptions); or a foreign patent application filed more than one year before the U.S. application. The prior reference disclosure need not use the same words as the claim but must disclose all requirements in enough detail to enable a skilled person to make and use the claimed invention. (See 35 U.S.C. §102(b), Pfaff, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (non‑statutory invalidity under Graham/KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid as obvious if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention at the relevant time. Even if no single prior art reference anticipates, the combination of prior art may render the claim obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not determine obviousness with hindsight; put yourself in the position of a person of ordinary skill at the time. Consider whether there was a reason that would have prompted such a person to combine prior art elements as the claimed invention does (teachings, suggestions, motivations may come from written references or the ordinary skill knowledge, or from the nature of the problem). Additional factual inquiries: (1) level of ordinary skill in the art; (2) scope and content of the prior art (what references are pertinent/analogous); (3) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art. Consider whether the innovation applied a known technique used to improve a similar device/method, or whether it would have been obvious to try (a small number of predictable options with reasonable expectation of success). Also consider secondary factors tending to show nonobviousness (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, unsuccessful attempts by others, copying, unexpected results, acceptance/licensing, prior art criticizing the invention) and factors tending to show obviousness (e.g., independent invention by others). The asserted invalidity must be proven highly probable by the party asserting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — alternative instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative phrasing of the obviousness instruction emphasizing the court's responsibility to determine obviousness based on jury findings of several factual questions and that the party asserting invalidity bears the burden to establish it is highly probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where matters are in dispute, the party asserting invalidity must establish its version of the factual questions (level of skill, scope/content of prior art, differences) as highly probable. (Reference to KSR and the court's gatekeeping role.)
